issues.passage: Critics questioned the plan’s efficacy after learning it would cost less than anyone expected.
issues.why: “Questioned the plan’s efficacy” is natural, correct use of efficacy = ability to produce a desired result. Low cost is a weak reason to doubt it, but the word itself is used properly.

fix.correctPassage: Researchers measured the vaccine’s efficacy by tracking infection rates in both trial groups.
wrongPassages: The committee praised the report’s efficacy, noting how carefully each footnote had been formatted.
They celebrated the drug’s efficacy when infection rates rose faster than in the control group.
Her speech’s efficacy was obvious once every listener left unconvinced and no vote shifted.

issues.passage: Her speech gained efficacy when she lowered her voice and avoided any claim of results.
issues.why: A speech can gain efficacy (become more effective) through delivery; lowering her voice is a plausible path to greater persuasive force. Avoiding result-claims does not make the usage incorrect.
